newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish cabinet split over restoring death penalty.
newsitem.headline: Polish cabinet split over restoring death penalty.

text.p: Poland's cabinet was deeply divided on Tuesday over calls to restore the death penalty in response to a series of particularly ugly murders.
Interior minister Leszek Miller, a member of the dominant ex-communist party in the ruling coalition, told a news conference that potential murderers had to be deterred.
"We often say that the death penalty is not carried out in Poland, but it is -- by murderers on innocent people," Miller said. "Society should be able to reply in kind."
But the non-party Justice Minister Leszek Kubicki argued against, telling the same conference that the best deterrent was to ensure criminals were caught and the law enforced.

On Monday thousands of citizens marched through Warsaw in a protest against criminal violence, prompted by the torture and killing this month of a 19-year-old student by a gang angry that he had attended a picnic in woods they saw as their turf.

Several of Miller's fellow ex-communist deputies, mindful of voters' opinion before September 21 general elections, have backed his call and his Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) party said it would leave the decision to members' consciences.

But Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, leading the party's campaign, opposed restoring the death sentence, which had been suspended since just before the 1989 fall of communism and was scrapped in a new criminal code approved by parliament this month.
"I am convinced the death penalty does not solve problems," Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told public radio, arguing for society to address wider origins of violent crime.
The death penalty is also opposed by Poland's influential Roman Catholic Church and by most of the centre and leftist opposition, but backed by parts of the right.
Miller, recognising the cabinet could not agree on a move to restore the death penalty, said he would try to muster support among parliamentary deputies to initiate an amendment.

In the meanwhile, the cabinet decided on Tuesday to allocate more funds to police and to try to make broadcasters obey a law banning them from showing violence at times when young people were watching television.
Justice Minister Kubicki argued that if Poland did restore executions, it would not be able to ratify article six of the European Convention on Human Rights.
He also said that despite popular perceptions, the number of murders was not rising and totalled 1,134 in 1995 and 1996.
In Poland the rate of murders per 100,000 people was 3.1, lower for instance than in France where it was four.
Overall crime rates in Poland are still below those of most Western European countries and the former Soviet states but they have risen steeply since the 1989 fall of communism.
But a number of senseless murders, some of promising students by youth gangs, have fuelled support for restoring the supreme penalty which is backed by a majority of Poles.

Monday's law and order march in Warsaw was the latest of more than a dozen around Poland since last year, each prompted by a killing starting with that of a student thrown from a moving train by hooligans in the port city Gdansk.
The last execution in Poland, by hanging, was carried out in 1988.
